front: Define **Kaiser**.
back: The **Kaiser** was the German word for 'King', the title of the ruler who held dictatorial power over Germany before 1918.

front: Define **Armistice**.
back: An **armistice** is an agreement to stop fighting, which Germany signed with the Allies on 11th November 1918 to end the First World War.

front: Define **Abdication**.
back: **Abdication** is when a ruler gives up their throne, as Kaiser Wilhelm II did on 9th November 1918 before fleeing to the Netherlands.

front: Define **Proportional representation**.
back: **Proportional representation** was the Weimar voting system in which one seat was equivalent to 60,000 votes, ensuring smaller parties were represented in the Reichstag.

front: How many German soldiers died between 1914 and 1918?
back: Between 1914 and 1918, **two million** German soldiers died and four million more were wounded.

front: Who became Chancellor of the new Weimar Republic after the Kaiser abdicated?
back: **Friedrich Ebert**, the leader of the SPD, became Chancellor of the new Weimar Republic after the Kaiser abdicated.

front: In which town did the National Assembly meet to write the constitution?
back: The National Assembly met in the town of **Weimar** to write the constitution, giving the Weimar Republic its name.

front: How many times did Ebert use Article 48 between 1923 and 1924?
back: Ebert used Article 48 **63 times** between 1923 and 1924.

front: What body did Ebert create to govern Germany until elections could be held?
back: Ebert created the **Council of People's Representatives**, six politicians who would govern Germany until elections could be held.

front: Germany's debt trebled from 50 billion marks in 1914 to <u>  </u> billion marks in 1918.
back: Germany's debt trebled from 50 billion marks in 1914 to **150** billion marks in 1918.

front: On 9th November 1918, the Kaiser's military advisers told him he must <u>     </u> to stop the civil unrest.
back: On 9th November 1918, the Kaiser's military advisers told him he must **abdicate** to stop the civil unrest.

front:
**True or False?**

The German navy mutinied in the ports of Kiel and Hamburg in October 1918.
back:
**True.**

In October 1918, the German navy mutinied in the ports of Kiel and Hamburg, part of the wave of civil unrest in the Revolution of 1918.

front:
**True or False?**

The SPD won a clear majority in the January 1919 elections.
back:
**False.**

The SPD won 40% of the vote but lacked a majority, so they had to rule in a coalition government with other parties.

front: Define **Reparations**.
back: **Reparations** were payments Germany had to make to the Allies as a condition of surrender, set at 132 billion gold marks (£6.6 billion).

front: Define **Dolchstoss**.
back: **Dolchstoss** means a 'stab in the back', the idea that German politicians had betrayed the country by signing the Treaty of Versailles.

front: Define **Anschluss**.
back: **Anschluss** was the union between Germany and Austria, which Article 80 of the Treaty of Versailles forbade.

front: Define **Hyperinflation**.
back: **Hyperinflation** is when prices rise rapidly and become out of control, as happened in Germany in 1923.

front: Which article of the Treaty of Versailles was the 'War Guilt' Clause?
back: **Article 231** was the 'War Guilt' Clause, forcing Germany to accept responsibility for starting the First World War.

front: To how many men was Germany's army restricted under the Treaty of Versailles?
back: Germany's army was restricted to **100,000 men** under Article 160 of the Treaty of Versailles.

front: What nickname was given to the politicians who signed the Treaty of Versailles?
back: The politicians who signed the Treaty of Versailles were called the **'November Criminals'**.

front: Who led the Spartacist Uprising of January 1919?
back: The Spartacist Uprising was led by **Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht**.

front: Which region did the French and Belgian armies occupy when Germany failed to pay reparations?
back: The French and Belgian armies occupied the **Ruhr** region of Germany.

front: The Treaty of Versailles set Germany's reparations at 132 billion <u>  </u> marks.
back: The Treaty of Versailles set Germany's reparations at 132 billion **gold** marks.

front: Ebert ordered the Reichswehr to organise <u>     </u> units to fight the Spartacist Uprising.
back: Ebert ordered the Reichswehr to organise **Freikorps** units to fight the Spartacist Uprising.

front:
**True or False?**

The Kapp Putsch was a right-wing challenge to the Weimar Republic.
back:
**True.**

The Kapp Putsch was a right-wing challenge to the Weimar Republic, whereas the Spartacist Uprising was a left-wing challenge.

front:
**True or False?**

The most extreme version of left-wing politics is Fascism.
back:
**False.**

The most extreme version of the left-wing is Communism; Fascism is the most extreme version of the right-wing.

front: Define **Rentenmark**.
back: The **Rentenmark** was the new currency introduced by Stresemann in November 1923, worth one trillion of the old marks and backed by the gold standard.

front: Define **Dawes Plan**.
back: The **Dawes Plan** of 1924 restructured Germany's reparations and brought US foreign investment into German industry.

front: Define **Young Plan**.
back: The **Young Plan** of 1929 reduced total reparations to £2 billion and extended the repayment period to 59 years.

front: Define **Kellogg-Briand Pact**.
back: The **Kellogg-Briand Pact** of 1928 was an agreement, signed by Germany and 61 other countries, that war should never be used to resolve disputes.

front: When did Stresemann become chancellor of Germany?
back: Stresemann became chancellor of Germany in **August 1923**.

front: In which year did Germany join the League of Nations?
back: Germany joined the League of Nations as a permanent member in **1926**.

front: What did Stresemann say Germany was doing in 1929 to describe its economic dependence on the USA?
back: In 1929 Stresemann stated that Germany was **'dancing on a volcano'**, because its economy depended on the US economy.

front: Which prize did Stresemann win in 1926?
back: Stresemann won the **Nobel Peace Prize** in 1926.

front: Who replaced Friedrich Ebert as president in 1925?
back: **Paul von Hindenburg** replaced Friedrich Ebert as president in 1925.

front: As a result of the Locarno Treaties, in September 1926 Stresemann obtained German membership of the <u>    </u> of Nations.
back: As a result of the Locarno Treaties, in September 1926 Stresemann obtained German membership of the **League** of Nations.

front: The Locarno Treaties were signed in December <u>  </u>, improving Germany's relationship with Europe.
back: The Locarno Treaties were signed in December **1925**, improving Germany's relationship with Europe.

front:
**True or False?**

One Rentenmark was the equivalent of a trillion old marks.
back:
**True.**

One Rentenmark was the equivalent of a trillion old marks, restoring a stable currency to Germany.

front:
**True or False?**

Stresemann died in office on 3rd October 1929.
back:
**True.**

Stresemann died in office of a heart attack on 3rd October 1929, shortly before the Wall Street Crash.

front: Define **Bauhaus**.
back: **Bauhaus** was a design movement founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 that used geometric shapes and materials such as concrete to create practical buildings.

front: Define **Welfare state**.
back: A **welfare state** is the concept that the government supports and improves the well-being of its citizens.

front: Define **New Woman**.
back: The **'New Woman'** of the 1920s was independent, career-minded and reluctant to become a wife or mother.

front: Define **Expressionism**.
back: **Expressionism** in Weimar Germany used grotesque or exaggerated figures in violent scenes to make the audience uncomfortable and question their society.

front: Who founded the Bauhaus movement?
back: **Walter Gropius** founded the Bauhaus movement in Weimar Germany in 1919.

front: Which 1922 Weimar film was the world's first vampire film?
back: **Nosferatu**, directed by F. W. Murnau in 1922, was the world's first vampire film.

front: What did the Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 pay an insured German who could not work?
back: The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1927 paid an insured German who could not work **60 Reichsmarks per week**.

front: At what age could all women vote under the Weimar Constitution?
back: Under the Weimar Constitution, all women over the age of **21** could vote, the same access as German men.

front: Which movement protested against the progression of Weimar society and wanted a return to traditional values?
back: The **Wandervögel** movement protested against the progression of Weimar society and wanted a return to traditional values.

front: The Weimar government funded the 1926 science-fiction film <u>      </u> through an organisation called UFA.
back: The Weimar government funded the 1926 science-fiction film **Metropolis** through an organisation called UFA.

front: By 1929, the income of <u>       </u> workers was 44% below the national average.
back: By 1929, the income of **agricultural** workers was 44% below the national average.

front:
**True or False?**

By 1925, the employment rate of women had fallen to 36%.
back:
**True.**

By 1925, the employment rate of women had fallen to 36%, roughly the same as before the First World War.

front:
**True or False?**

The Nazi Party (NSDAP) supported the experimental culture of the Weimar Republic.
back:
**False.**

The NSDAP believed Weimar culture was destroying German traditions and was responsible for the moral decline of German society.

front: Define **DAP**.
back: The **DAP** (German Workers' Party) was a right-wing party founded by **Anton Drexler** in February 1919 that targeted the working classes.

front: Who founded the DAP and in what month and year?
back: The DAP was founded by **Anton Drexler in February 1919**.

front: Why did the German government first send Hitler to attend a DAP meeting?
back: The government sent Hitler to **spy on political parties** in Munich and report how dangerous they were.

front: Hitler attended his first DAP meeting on 12th September 1919 and signed up as a member on <u>  </u> September 1919.
back: Hitler attended his first DAP meeting on 12th September 1919 and signed up as a member on **19th** September 1919.

front: Define **Twenty-Five Point Programme**.
back: The **Twenty-Five Point Programme** was the political programme written by Hitler and Drexler in January 1920 that formalised the party's aims, mixing **nationalist and socialist** ideas.

front: What did the NSDAP stand for?
back: The NSDAP stood for the **National Socialist German Workers' Party**.

front:
**True or False?**

By June 1920, the DAP had 1,000 members.
back:
**True.**

The DAP grew rapidly in 1920, reaching **1,000 members** by June 1920 and 3,000 by the end of the year, mainly due to the appeal of Hitler.

front: Define **orator**.
back: An **orator** is a skilled public speaker; Hitler's skill as an **orator** persuaded audiences and increased Nazi Party membership.

front: Which contest did Hitler trigger in July 1921?
back: In July 1921, Hitler triggered a **leadership contest**, which he won by defeating **Drexler** to gain control of the NSDAP.

front: Define **SA**.
back: The **SA** (Sturmabteilung), nicknamed the '**Brownshirts**', was the NSDAP's private army, formed in August 1921.

front: In January 1922, Hitler called a party conference at which he established his <u>      </u> control of the NSDAP.
back: In January 1922, Hitler called a party conference at which he established his **autocratic** control of the NSDAP.

front: How many members did the NSDAP have by November 1923?
back: By November 1923, the NSDAP had **50,000 members**.

front: Define **The Lean Years**.
back: **The Lean Years** is the term historians use for 1924-1928, when the German people considered the **NSDAP a small, extremist group** after the Munich Putsch.

front: In which month and year did Hitler launch the Munich Putsch?
back: Hitler launched the Munich Putsch in **November 1923**.

front: Which respected military veteran did Hitler include in the putsch to rally army support?
back: Hitler included **General Ludendorff** in the putsch to rally the support of the army.

front: Which crime were Hitler and Ludendorff tried for after the putsch?
back: Hitler and Ludendorff went on trial for **high treason**.

front: What was the title of the book Hitler wrote in Landsberg Prison?
back: In Landsberg Prison, Hitler wrote a book called ***Mein Kampf*** ('My Struggle').

front: Hitler served only <u>  </u> months of his five-year sentence before being released from prison.
back: Hitler served only **nine** months of his five-year sentence before being released from prison.

front: Define **Lebensraum**.
back: **Lebensraum** means '**living space**'; Hitler theorised that the Aryan race needed more territory, taken from Eastern Europe, so the population could grow.

front: Define **gauleiter**.
back: A **gauleiter** was the local Nazi Party leader in charge of one of the 35 regions (gaue) into which Hitler divided Germany.

front: Who became head of the SS?
back: **Heinrich Himmler** became head of the SS.

front: In which Bavarian town did Hitler hold a party conference in 1926?
back: Hitler held the 1926 party conference in **Bamberg**, Bavaria.

front:
**True or False?**

In the May 1928 election, the Nazi Party won 12 seats in the Reichstag.
back:
**True.**

In the May 1928 election, the Nazi Party won only **12 seats** (roughly 3% of votes), making them the seventh biggest party in the Reichstag.

front: By 1929, the NSDAP had <u>    </u> members, yet historians still call this period 'The Lean Years'.
back: By 1929, the NSDAP had **100,000** members, yet historians still call this period 'The Lean Years'.

front: In what month and year did Hitler become Chancellor of Germany?
back: Hitler became Chancellor of Germany in **January 1933**.

front: Which event triggered the economic collapse in Germany known as the Depression?
back: The **Wall Street Crash** triggered economic collapses across Europe, including Germany.

front: By January 1933, unemployment in Germany had reached <u>  </u> million people.
back: By January 1933, unemployment in Germany had reached **6.1** million people.

front: Who organised Hitler's political campaigns in 1930 and 1932?
back: **Goebbels** organised Hitler's political campaigns in 1930 and 1932.

front: Which party did Chancellor Heinrich Brüning lead?
back: Heinrich Brüning was the leader of the **Centre Party**.

front: On what date did Brüning resign as Chancellor?
back: Brüning resigned on **30th May 1932**, having lost majority support in the Reichstag.

front: What nickname did the German public give von Papen's government?
back: The German public called von Papen's government '**the Cabinet of Barons**'.

front: What share of the vote did the Nazi Party receive in the July 1932 election?
back: In the July 1932 election, the Nazi Party received **38%** of the vote, becoming the biggest party in the Reichstag.

front:
**True or False?**

In the November 1932 election, the Nazi share of the vote fell to 33%.
back:
**True.**

In the November 1932 election, the NSDAP's share of the vote reduced to **33%**, though they remained the biggest party.

front: On what date did Hindenburg appoint von Schleicher as Chancellor?
back: Hindenburg appointed von Schleicher as Chancellor on **2nd December 1932**.

front: Von Schleicher asked Hindenburg to suspend the constitution so he could form a <u>     </u> dictatorship.
back: Von Schleicher asked Hindenburg to suspend the constitution so he could form a **military** dictatorship.

front: Define **co-chancellor**.
back: A **co-chancellor** was the role von Papen proposed for himself alongside Hitler's chancellorship, believing he could control Hitler and make the real decisions for Germany.

front: On what date did the Reichstag building burn down?
back: The Reichstag building burnt down on **27th February 1933**.

front: Who was arrested at the scene of the Reichstag Fire?
back: A Dutch Communist named **Marinus van der Lubbe** was arrested at the scene and later executed.

front: Define **Reichstag Fire Decree**.
back: The **Reichstag Fire Decree** was an emergency law that let Hitler scapegoat the KPD, imprison political opponents and shut down Communist newspapers.

front: What share of the vote did the Nazis win in the March 1933 election?
back: The Nazis won nearly **44%** of the vote, still short of the two-thirds majority needed to change the constitution.

front: The <u>     </u> Act became law on 24th March 1933, letting Hitler's cabinet pass laws without the Reichstag's approval.
back: The **Enabling** Act became law on 24th March 1933, letting Hitler's cabinet pass laws without the Reichstag's approval.

front: By how many votes was the Enabling Act passed?
back: The Enabling Act was passed by **444 votes to 94**.

front:
**True or False?**

Only the SPD opposed the Enabling Act vote.
back:
**True.**

Only the **SPD** opposed the vote; all 81 Communist Party members were absent and the SA intimidated other Reichstag members.

front: What did the German Labour Front replace in May 1933?
back: The Nazi-controlled **German Labour Front** replaced the abolished **trade unions** in May 1933.

front: In July 1933, all political parties except the <u>   </u> were banned, creating a one-party state.
back: In July 1933, all political parties except the **NSDAP** were banned, creating a one-party state.

front: On what date did the Night of the Long Knives take place?
back: The Night of the Long Knives took place on **30th June 1934**.

front: Which SA leader was arrested and shot during the Night of the Long Knives?
back: **Ernst Röhm**, head of the SA, was arrested and later shot, along with around 400 SA members.

front: Define **Führer**.
back: **Führer** was the title Hitler took after Hindenburg's death on 2nd August 1934, when he **combined the positions of president and chancellor**.

front: Define **Confessing Church**.
back: The **Confessing Church** was a section of the German Protestant community, created by **Pastor Martin Niemöller**, that opposed Nazi interference in the Church and the Reich Church.

front: Define **Edelweiss Pirates**.
back: The **Edelweiss Pirates** were a youth group who passively and violently resisted the **Hitler Youth**, going on camping trips and singing folk songs.

front: Define **Swing Youth**.
back: The **Swing Youth** were a group of young people who opposed the Nazis by listening to **jazz music**, which Hitler had banned.

front: Define **White Rose group**.
back: The **White Rose group** was formed at Munich University in 1943 and publicly opposed the Nazi government through **anti-Nazi leaflets** and marches.

front: Who created the Confessing Church?
back: The Confessing Church was created by **Pastor Martin Niemöller**.

front: Which cardinal led the Catholic opposition against the Nazis' T-4 programme?
back: The Catholic opposition against the Nazis' T-4 programme was led by **Cardinal Galen**.

front: Who brought a briefcase bomb into Wolf's Lair in the July 1944 Plot?
back: The briefcase bomb was brought into Wolf's Lair by army officer **Claus von Stauffenberg**.

front: Who were the leaders of the White Rose group?
back: The leaders of the White Rose group were **Hans and Sophie Scholl**, who were arrested and executed by guillotine in 1943.

front: Which event in 1943 marked a turning point that increased opposition to the Nazis?
back: Germany's **poor performance in the Second World War** marked a turning point in 1943 that increased opposition from more areas of society.

front: The main youth opposition group in Germany was the Edelweiss <u>      </u>, whose Cologne members killed the Gestapo chief in 1944.
back: The main youth opposition group in Germany was the Edelweiss **Pirates**, whose Cologne members killed the Gestapo chief in 1944.

front: Most opposition to the Nazis was <u>      </u> because it was incredibly dangerous to openly oppose the regime.
back: Most opposition to the Nazis was **private** because it was incredibly dangerous to openly oppose the regime.

front:
**True or False?**

By July 1933, all political parties and trade unions had been banned in Germany.
back:
**True.**

By July 1933 all political parties and trade unions were banned, which helped eliminate the strongest open opposition.

front: Define **Gestapo**.
back: The **Gestapo** were the Nazi secret police who wore plain clothes, tapped phones, arrested and tortured suspects, and sent people to concentration camps.

front: Define **SD**.
back: The **SD** was the Nazi intelligence agency, created by Heinrich Himmler in 1931, that gathered information on suspected opponents of the Nazi Party.

front: Define **Concordat**.
back: The **Concordat** was an agreement signed between Hitler and the Pope in July 1933, allowing Catholics to worship freely in return for priests not interfering in politics.

front: Define **Reich Church**.
back: The **Reich Church** was the unified Protestant Church led by Reich Bishop **Ludwig Müller**, which displayed the swastika and barred Jewish people from baptism.

front: Who became leader of the SS from 1929?
back: The leader of the SS from 1929 was **Heinrich Himmler**.

front: Who was placed in charge of the SD?
back: The SD was placed under the charge of **Reinhard Heydrich**.

front: What was the first concentration camp in Nazi Germany?
back: The first concentration camp in Nazi Germany was **Dachau**, which opened in 1933.

front: Which court was introduced to hear cases of treason?
back: The court introduced to hear cases of treason was the **People's Court**.

front: Who became Reich Bishop of the Reich Church?
back: The Reich Bishop of the Reich Church was **Ludwig Müller**.

front: The SS was created in <u>      </u> to act as personal bodyguards to Hitler.
back: The SS was created in **1925** to act as personal bodyguards to Hitler.

front: The Nazis removed trial by <u>      </u> so that judges could decide the outcome of a case.
back: The Nazis removed trial by **jury** so that judges could decide the outcome of a case.

front:
**True or False?**

Around 80% of political crimes were reported to the Gestapo by ordinary citizens.
back:
**True.**

Only around 10% of political crimes were discovered by the Gestapo, compared to 80% reported by ordinary citizens, showing the regime's reliance on denunciations.

front: Define **Volksempfänger**.
back: The **Volksempfänger**, or People's Receiver, was one of Europe's cheapest radios, introduced in 1933 with a short range so foreign stations could not be picked up.

front: Define **Reich Chamber of Culture**.
back: The **Reich Chamber of Culture** was a body set up in 1933 to ensure all aspects of culture and the arts aligned with Nazi beliefs.

front: Define **Der Völkischer Beobachter**.
back: **Der Völkischer Beobachter**, or The People's Observer, was the official daily newspaper of the Nazi Party, reaching 1.1 million people by 1941.

front: What was Joseph Goebbels' official government title?
back: Joseph Goebbels was the **Minister for People's Enlightenment and Propaganda**.

front: Which city hosted the annual Nazi rallies from 1933 to 1938?
back: The annual Nazi rallies from 1933 to 1938 were hosted in **Nuremberg**.

front: Who designed the grounds where the Nuremberg rallies took place?
back: The grounds where the Nuremberg rallies took place were designed by Hitler's favourite architect, **Albert Speer**.

front: Which athlete angered Hitler by winning four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics?
back: The athlete who angered Hitler by winning four gold medals was **Jesse Owens**.

front: Which director filmed the Nuremberg rally footage used in Triumph of the Will?
back: The director who filmed Triumph of the Will was **Leni Riefenstahl**.

front: Why did the Nazis dislike jazz music?
back: The Nazis disliked jazz music because it was **associated with Black people**, and many jazz artists were also of Jewish origins.

front: The 1934 Nuremberg rally used 152 searchlights as pillars of light, known as the <u>      </u> of Light.
back: The 1934 Nuremberg rally used 152 searchlights as pillars of light, known as the **Cathedral** of Light.

front: In May 1933, students in Berlin burned around <u>      </u> books by anti-Nazi authors.
back: In May 1933, students in Berlin burned around **20,000** books by anti-Nazi authors.

front:
**True or False?**

The Nazis controlled most German newspapers by 1939.
back:
**True.**

The Nazis controlled most newspapers by 1939, compared to only 3% in 1933, and around 1,600 newspapers were closed down in 1935.

front: Define **eugenics**.
back: **Eugenics** was the science of selective breeding, which the Nazis used to encourage the 'best' Germans to reproduce and prevent those they considered 'undesirable'.

front: Define **Untermenschen**.
back: **Untermenschen** (sub-humans) was the Nazi term for races of Eastern Europe, such as the Slavs, whom they viewed as inferior.

front: Define **Nuremberg Laws**.
back: The **Nuremberg Laws** of 1935 were two laws that stripped Jewish people of German citizenship and banned them from marrying German citizens.

front: Define **Kristallnacht**.
back: **Kristallnacht** (Night of Broken Glass) was a nationwide attack on Jewish communities in November 1938, during which synagogues, shops and homes were destroyed.

front: Which race did the Nazis regard as superior in their racial hierarchy?
back: The Nazis regarded the **Aryan** race as superior, describing them as blonde, blue-eyed and athletic.

front: What did the T-4 Programme use to kill disabled people?
back: The T-4 Programme killed disabled people using **carbon monoxide**, and historians estimate it killed 250,000 people.

front: On what date were the Nuremberg Laws introduced?
back: The Nuremberg Laws were introduced on **15 September 1935**.

front: At the Wannsee Conference, what did the Nazis agree upon?
back: At the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, the Nazis agreed upon the **'Final Solution of the Jewish Question'**, which began the development of extermination camps.

front: What symbol were homosexuals forced to wear for identification in concentration camps?
back: Homosexuals were forced to wear a **pink triangle** for identification in concentration camps.

front: After Kristallnacht, Jewish people were forced to pay a combined total of <u>      </u> marks to repair the damage.
back: After Kristallnacht, Jewish people were forced to pay a combined total of **1 billion** marks to repair the damage.

front: From 1939, Jewish people were forcibly evicted from their homes and placed into <u>      </u>.
back: From 1939, Jewish people were forcibly evicted from their homes and placed into **ghettos**.

front:
**True or False?**

The Nazis viewed Jewish people as a religion rather than a race.
back:
**False.**

The Nazis considered Jewish people to be a race, not a religion, meaning no Jewish person could escape persecution whether they practised Judaism or not.

front: Define **totalitarianism**.
back: **Totalitarianism** is a government that has complete control over its citizens.

front: How did fear support the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state?
back: **Fear stopped many Germans from opposing the Nazis**, which supports the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: How did informing on others support the idea of a totalitarian state?
back: Many Germans **actively informed on their friends and family**, which supports the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: How did propaganda support the argument for a totalitarian state?
back: **Propaganda made people support the Nazi Party**, which supports the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: How did youth organisations challenge the idea of a totalitarian state?
back: **Many youth organisations challenged the Nazi Party's ideology**, which challenges the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: How did the T-4 programme challenge the idea of a totalitarian state?
back: **The public spoke out against the T-4 programme**, which challenges the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: Which institution provided continual opposition, challenging the idea of a totalitarian state?
back: The Nazis faced continual opposition from the **Church**, which challenges the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: Define **conformity**.
back: **Conformity** refers to the way many Germans went along with the Nazi regime, which supports the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: The argument against a totalitarian state notes that the Nazis had to use <u>      </u> to maintain control.
back: The argument against a totalitarian state notes that the Nazis had to use **force** to maintain control.

front: Supporting the totalitarian argument, many Germans did not protect <u>      </u> groups.
back: Supporting the totalitarian argument, many Germans did not protect **minority** groups.

front:
**True or False?**

Opposition existed within the German army, challenging the idea of a totalitarian state.
back:
**True.**

Opposition existed in the army, which is used as evidence to challenge the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front:
**True or False?**

Agreement with Nazi racial policy is used as evidence that Germany was a totalitarian state.
back:
**True.**

Many people agreed with the Nazis' racial policy, which is used as evidence to support the argument that Germany was a totalitarian state.

front: Define **Hitler Youth**.
back: The **Hitler Youth** was the Nazi youth group for boys aged 14 to 18, which focused on physical and military training to create an army for the future.

front: Define **League of German Maidens**.
back: The **League of German Maidens** (Bund Deutscher Mädel) was the female equivalent of the Hitler Youth, which trained girls aged 14 to 18 to be good wives and mothers.

front: Define **Napolas**.
back: **Napolas** were Nazi schools for the most 'gifted' and racially pure children, where SS members replaced traditional teachers and students went on to join the SS or police services.

front: Define **Faith and Beauty Society**.
back: The **Faith and Beauty Society** was a sub-group of the BDM created in 1938 for girls aged 17 to 21, which provided further education until they were old enough to join the National Socialist Women's League.

front: Who was the leader of the Hitler Youth?
back: The leader of the Hitler Youth was **Baldur von Schirach**.

front: Who was made Education Minister in 1934?
back: The person made Education Minister in 1934 was **Bernhard Rust**.

front: Why did the Nazis want to control the youth of Germany?
back: The Nazis wanted to control the youth because young people were easier to influence than adults, ensuring the **Nazi Party would always have public support**.

front: Which text became a compulsory text in Nazi schools?
back: The text that became a compulsory text in Nazi schools was **Mein Kampf**.

front: What did the Nazis want to create for the future through the Hitler Youth?
back: The Nazis wanted to create an **army for the future** to ensure the protection of Nazi Germany.

front: By 1939, membership of the Nazi youth groups had reached <u>       </u> members.
back: By 1939, membership of the Nazi youth groups had reached **nine million** members.

front: All teachers were expected to join the Nazi <u>     </u> League.
back: All teachers were expected to join the Nazi **Teachers'** League.

front:
**True or False?**

Boys and girls were taught together in Nazi schools.
back:
**False.**

Boys and girls were educated separately in Nazi Germany.

front: Define **Lebensborn Programme**.
back: The **Lebensborn Programme** was a scheme started in 1935 by Heinrich Himmler that paired SS men with single women of clear 'Aryan' ancestry to create 'genetically pure' children.

front: Define **German Women's Enterprise**.
back: The **German Women's Enterprise** (DFW) was the organisation all women-related groups had to join, which enrolled members on courses about childcare, cooking and sewing.

front: Define **Mother's Cross**.
back: The **Mother's Cross** was an award presented on Mother's Day to women who had four or more children, with a gold medal earning a public salute from the Hitler Youth.

front: Define the **'three Ks'**.
back: The **'three Ks'** were Kinder (children), Kirche (church) and Küche (cooking), which the Nazis believed a woman's life should revolve around.

front: Who oversaw all Nazi policies related to women?
back: All Nazi policies related to women were overseen by **Gertrud Scholtz-Klink**.

front: How much was the loan offered under the 1933 Law for the Encouragement of Marriage?
back: The loan offered under the 1933 Law for the Encouragement of Marriage was **1,000 marks**, equivalent to eight months' wages.

front: Why did the Nazis want to increase the birth rate?
back: The Nazis wanted to increase the birth rate because the **First World War had caused a decline in the male population** and the birth rate had fallen to one million births per year by 1933.

front: From which professional jobs were women banned in 1933?
back: In 1933, women were banned from being **teachers, doctors and other professional posts**.

front: How did the number of marriages change between 1932 and 1934?
back: The number of marriages increased from **500,000 in 1932 to 750,000 by 1934**.

front: Under the 1935 Lebensborn Programme, only around 7,000 children were <u>  </u>.
back: Under the 1935 Lebensborn Programme, only around 7,000 children were **born**.

front: During the Second World War, 2.4 million women returned to <u>  </u>.
back: During the Second World War, 2.4 million women returned to **work**.

front:
**True or False?**

Mothers who gave birth to four children had to repay their marriage loan in full.
back:
**False.**

Mothers who gave birth to four children did not have to pay the loan back, as each child removed a quarter of the loan.

front: Define **Labour Front**.
back: The **Labour Front** (DAF) was the organisation that replaced trade unions after 1933 and controlled the rights, hours and pay levels of workers.

front: Define **Strength Through Joy**.
back: **Strength Through Joy** (KdF) was a Nazi organisation established in 1933 that provided out-of-work leisure activities, trips and holidays to make work seem more enjoyable and prevent unrest.

front: Define **Beauty of Labour**.
back: **Beauty of Labour** (SdA) was a Nazi programme created in 1934 that aimed to provide better facilities for workers, such as toilets, changing rooms, showers and canteens.

front: Define **invisible unemployment**.
back: **Invisible unemployment** refers to people who do not have full-time jobs but are not counted in official unemployment statistics.

front: Who did Hitler appoint as Minister of the Economy?
back: Hitler appointed **Dr Schacht** as Minister of the Economy.

front: What was the affordable 'people's car' promised to workers called?
back: The affordable 'people's car' promised to workers was called the **Volkswagen**.

front: What farming mentality did the Nazis believe in?
back: The Nazis believed in the **'Blood and Soil'** mentality, valuing farmers much higher than urban workers.

front: Which law stopped banks repossessing farmers' property if they fell into debt?
back: The law that stopped banks repossessing farmers' property was the **Reich Entailed Farm Law**.

front: What did the National Labour Service provide for the unemployed?
back: The National Labour Service (RAD) provided **paid work** for the unemployed, such as repairing roads and planting trees.

front: In September 1933, Hitler personally started the project to build an <u>     </u> system across Germany.
back: In September 1933, Hitler personally started the project to build an **autobahn** system across Germany.

front: By 1939, food prices in Nazi Germany had increased by <u>  </u>.
back: By 1939, food prices in Nazi Germany had increased by **20%**.

front:
**True or False?**

The Nazis kept their promise to restrict large department stores for small business owners.
back:
**False.**

The government did not fulfil their promise, and large businesses still dominated the market.

front: Define **autarky**.
back: **Autarky** means economic self-sufficiency, which Hitler wanted so that a blockade would not destroy Germany's economy or food supply.

front: Define **ersatz goods**.
back: **Ersatz goods** were substitute products the Nazis increased under the Four Year Plan, such as using coal to make rubber and acorns to make coffee.

front: Define **Volkssturm**.
back: The **Volkssturm** ('people's storm') was a Home Guard of conscripted young and elderly men created by Hitler, which failed in battle.

front: Define the **Four Year Plan**.
back: The **Four Year Plan** was Goering's economic programme running from 1936 to 1939 that aimed to achieve autarky, increase farming output and rearmament, and impose more government control on industry.

front: Who did Hitler make Minister of the Economy in 1936?
back: In 1936, Hitler made **Hermann Goering** Minister of the Economy.

front: Who switched Germany to a war economy in 1942?
back: Germany was switched to a war economy in 1942 by **Albert Speer**, the new Minister of Armaments and War Production.

front: Which 1942 battle signified the war would not be quick for Germany?
back: The battle that signified the war would not be quick was the **Battle of Stalingrad**.

front: Roughly how many Jewish people died during the Holocaust?
back: Roughly **six million Jewish people** died during the Holocaust.

front: What did the indoctrinated Hitler Youth do after British aerial bombings?
back: The indoctrinated Hitler Youth enthusiastically helped **put out fires** after British aerial bombings.

front: A bombing raid on the city of <u>    </u> in February 1945 caused 150,000 civilian casualties.
back: A bombing raid on the city of **Dresden** in February 1945 caused 150,000 civilian casualties.

front: By 1944, one-quarter of Germany's <u>     </u> was enslaved.
back: By 1944, one-quarter of Germany's **workforce** was enslaved.

front:
**True or False?**

Germany had achieved full economic self-sufficiency by the outbreak of war in 1939.
back:
**False.**

Germany had not achieved autarky, and by 1939 it still imported one-third of its raw materials.

front: Define **Tsar**.
back: **Tsar** is the Russian word for 'King', the autocratic ruler of Russia.

front: Define **Slavophiles**.
back: **Slavophiles** were Russians who saw Russia as a special country that needed protection and who distrusted Europe.

front: Define **Westernisers**.
back: **Westernisers** were Russians who looked to Europe for inspiration and wanted to apply it to Russia.

front: Define **mir**.
back: A **mir** was a Russian village, where most Russians lived in 1905.

front: Which dynasty established control over Russia in 1613?
back: The dynasty that established control over Russia in 1613 was the **Romanov** dynasty.

front: What were the three 'pillars' that Russian society stood upon?
back: The three 'pillars' of Russian society were the **tsar, the Orthodox Church and the Army**.

front: In which year did Tsar Alexander II free the serfs through the Emancipation Edict?
back: Tsar Alexander II freed the serfs through the Emancipation Edict in **1861**.

front: Which calendar did Russia continue to use in 1905?
back: In 1905, Russia continued to use the **Julian Calendar**.

front: By 1905, <u>      </u> of Russia's population lived in the countryside.
back: By 1905, **87%** of Russia's population lived in the countryside.

front: More than <u>      </u> of Russia's population were illiterate.
back: More than **60%** of Russia's population were illiterate.

front:
**True or False?**

Russia had experienced an industrial revolution by 1905.
back:
**False.**

Russia had **not** experienced an industrial revolution, and its limited industry developed in the west of the empire.

front:
**True or False?**

The Russian Empire spanned both Europe and Asia.
back:
**True.**

The Russian Empire was nearly 5,000 kilometres wide and spanned both Europe and Asia.

front: Define **Okhrana**.
back: The **Okhrana** was the secret police in Tsarist Russia, which investigated, arrested and tortured suspects.

front: Define **zemstvo**.
back: A **zemstvo** was a rural council in the Russian Empire whose representatives were elected by the people.

front: Define **bourgeoisie**.
back: The **bourgeoisie** were the industrialists and business owners who had a lot of money but very little power.

front: Define **kulaks**.
back: **Kulaks** were the small number of peasants who could buy land through the Peasant Land Bank.

front: Which mountain range divided the Russian Empire?
back: The Russian Empire was divided by the **Ural Mountains**.

front: Who was the Finance Minister behind the 'Great Spurt' of the 1890s?
back: The Finance Minister behind the 'Great Spurt' of the 1890s was **Sergei Witte**.

front: Which railway did Russia begin constructing to develop its economy?
back: Russia began construction of the **Trans-Siberian Railway**.

front: Who wrote The Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital with Friedrich Engels?
back: The Communist Manifesto and Das Kapital were written by **Karl Marx** with Friedrich Engels.

front: Only <u>      </u> of the population of the Russian Empire was ethnic Russian.
back: Only **40%** of the population of the Russian Empire was ethnic Russian.

front: Around <u>      </u> of the population were peasants.
back: Around **80%** of the population were peasants.

front:
**True or False?**

Russia had an elected parliament, or duma, before 1905.
back:
**False.**

There was no elected parliament or duma, as the tsar did not believe his people should have the right to vote.

front:
**True or False?**

In 1903, the Social Democrats split into the Mensheviks and the Bolsheviks.
back:
**True.**

In 1903 the Social Democrats split into the Mensheviks ('Minority'), led by Martov, and the Bolsheviks ('Majority'), led by Lenin.

front: Define **Bloody Sunday**.
back: **Bloody Sunday** was the event on 22nd January 1905 when the army opened fire on protestors at the Winter Palace, starting the revolution.

front: Define **Soviets**.
back: **Soviets** were elected councils created by workers in major towns to represent their demands for better pay and working conditions.

front: Define **October Manifesto**.
back: The **October Manifesto** was Nicholas II's reform that promised an elected duma, more political rights and a change to the system of government.

front: Define **Russification**.
back: **Russification** was a policy under which non-Russian nationalities were unfairly treated, prompting them to want independence.

front: Who led the protestors to the Winter Palace on Bloody Sunday?
back: The protestors were led to the Winter Palace on Bloody Sunday by **Father Gapon**.

front: Which country defeated Russia in the war over Manchuria?
back: Russia was defeated in the war over Manchuria by **Japan**.

front: Whom did Nicholas choose as Prime Minister in 1906?
back: In 1906 Nicholas chose **Peter Stolypin** as Prime Minister.

front: Which crew mutinied in June 1905?
back: In June 1905 the sailors of the **battleship Potemkin** mutinied.

front: Bloody Sunday took place on 22nd January <u>      </u>.
back: Bloody Sunday took place on 22nd January **1905**.

front: The nickname for the noose used by Stolypin was 'Stolypin's <u>      </u>'.
back: The nickname for the noose used by Stolypin was 'Stolypin's **Necktie**'.

front:
**True or False?**

The Tsar allowed four dumas between 1906 and 1914.
back:
**True.**

The Tsar allowed four dumas between 1906 and 1914, closing down the first two radical ones and weakening the later two.

front:
**True or False?**

The 1905 Revolution resulted in the overthrow of the tsar.
back:
**False.**

The 1905 Revolution did not overthrow the tsar; Nicholas survived by using a combination of reform and repression.

front: Define **Brusilov Offensive**.
back: The **Brusilov Offensive** was the largest Russian attack of the First World War, launched in June 1916 against the Austro-Hungarian Army.

front: Define **desertion**.
back: **Desertion** was soldiers abandoning the army, and over one million Russian soldiers had deserted by 1917.

front: Define **haemophilia**.
back: **Haemophilia** was the illness of Alexei, the heir to the throne, which was kept secret from the Russian people.

front: Which 1914 battle destroyed the Russian Second Army?
back: The battle that destroyed the Russian Second Army in 1914 was the Battle of **Tannenberg**.

front: In which year did Tsar Nicholas II take personal command of the Russian Army?
back: Tsar Nicholas II took personal command of the Russian Army in **1915**.

front: What was St Petersburg renamed to in 1914?
back: In 1914, St Petersburg was renamed **Petrograd** because its name had Germanic roots.

front: Who acted as Tsarina Alexandra's adviser while Nicholas was at the front?
back: While Nicholas was at the front, Tsarina Alexandra's adviser was **Rasputin**.

front: In which month and year did Russian aristocrats murder Rasputin?
back: Russian aristocrats murdered Rasputin in **December 1916**.

front: By 1916, over <u>        </u> Russians had died in the conflict.
back: By 1916, over **1.7 million** Russians had died in the conflict.

front: During the First World War, inflation in Russia rose to <u>      </u>.
back: During the First World War, inflation in Russia rose to **200%**.

front:
**True or False?**

Tsarina Alexandra was German.
back:
**True.**

Tsarina Alexandra was German, and many people began to dislike the German influence on Russia.

front:
**True or False?**

Tsar Nicholas II had extensive military experience when he took command of the army.
back:
**False.**

Nicholas had no military experience, so the people could blame Russia's military defeats on the tsar.

front: Define **Dual Power**.
back: **Dual Power** was the system that replaced the Tsarist government after the March 1917 Revolution, shared between the Provisional Government and the Petrograd Soviet.

front: Define **abdication**.
back: **Abdication** was Tsar Nicholas II giving up the throne, which he did on 15th March 1917.

front: Define **Petrograd Soviet**.
back: The **Petrograd Soviet** was the body that represented the workers and took control of supplies in Petrograd during the March 1917 Revolution.

front: On what date did Tsar Nicholas II abdicate?
back: Tsar Nicholas II abdicated on **15th March 1917**.

front: Which steel workers went on strike from 7th-10th March 1917?
back: The workers who went on strike from 7th-10th March 1917 were the **Putilov** steel workers.

front: Who led the Provisional Government under Dual Power?
back: The Provisional Government under Dual Power was led by **Prince Lvov**.

front: Which two groups could govern Russia instead of the tsar?
back: The two groups that could govern Russia instead of the tsar were the **duma and the Soviets**.

front: The March 1917 Revolution is known as a 'revolution from <u>      </u>'.
back: The March 1917 Revolution is known as a 'revolution from **below**'.

front: The Putilov steel workers struck alongside women on International <u>        </u> Day.
back: The Putilov steel workers struck alongside women on International **Women's** Day.

front:
**True or False?**

The First World War turned the army against Tsar Nicholas.
back:
**True.**

The First World War turned the army against Tsar Nicholas, and without the army he lost his power.

front:
**True or False?**

Nicholas' brother Michael accepted the throne after the abdication.
back:
**False.**

Nicholas' brother refused the position, ending 300 years of the Romanov dynasty.

front: Why did the Provisional Government need the Petrograd Soviet?
back: The Provisional Government needed the Petrograd Soviet for their **influence over the Army and workers**.

front: Define **Provisional Government**.
back: The **Provisional Government** was a temporary government created by the duma with 12 representatives to fill the power vacuum after the Tsar abdicated in March 1917.

front: Define **Dual Power**.
back: **Dual Power** was the sharing of authority in Russia from March 1917 between the **Provisional Government** and the **Petrograd Soviet**.

front: Define **Soviet Order No.1**.
back: **Soviet Order No.1** was a directive released by the Petrograd Soviet that instructed the Russian Army to obey the **Petrograd Soviet** rather than the Provisional Government.

front: Who replaced Prince Lvov as Prime Minister in July 1917?
back: Prince Lvov was replaced as Prime Minister by **Kerensky** in July 1917.

front: Which general did Kerensky appoint as commander of the Russian Army?
back: Kerensky appointed **General Kornilov** as commander of the Russian Army.

front: Where did Lenin flee to after the July Days?
back: After the July Days, Lenin fled to **Finland** to avoid being arrested.

front: Which failed offensive did Kerensky launch as Minister of War?
back: As Minister of War, Kerensky launched the **June Offensive**, which failed to push back Austrian troops.

front: What did peasants begin doing by mid-1917 over the land issue?
back: By mid-1917, the peasants began **illegally seizing land** because the Provisional Government delayed making a decision.

front: During the Kornilov Affair, Kerensky armed the <u>     </u> so they could defend Petrograd.
back: During the Kornilov Affair, Kerensky armed the **Red Guard** so they could defend Petrograd.

front: The Provisional Government continued Russia's involvement in the First World War because it needed British and <u>    </u> investment.
back: The Provisional Government continued Russia's involvement in the First World War because it needed British and **French** investment.

front:
**True or False?**

Lenin led the Bolsheviks in support of the July Days.
back:
**False.**

Lenin refused to support the July Days, unsure if the time was right, and many historians criticise this decision.

front:
**True or False?**

The Provisional Government confirmed a firm date for national elections.
back:
**False.**

The Provisional Government wanted elections to give them a mandate but never confirmed a date for them.

front: Define **April Theses**.
back: The **April Theses** was a speech made by Lenin when he returned to Petrograd in April 1917, outlining his key policies of 'Peace, Bread, Land!' and 'All power to the Soviets!'.

front: Define **sealed train**.
back: The **sealed train** was the train on which Lenin travelled back to Russia through countries without passport checks, with his journey funded by Germany.

front: Define **coup**.
back: A **coup** is a sudden seizure of power by a small group, which is how historians consider the events of the October Revolution.

front: Who was the leader of the Bolshevik Party who pushed for the revolution?
back: The leader of the Bolshevik Party who pushed for the revolution was **Lenin**.

front: Which Bolshevik organised the revolution and was known for his oration skills?
back: The revolution was organised by **Trotsky**, who was known for his oration skills.

front: Which two key Bolsheviks voted against the October Revolution?
back: **Zinoviev and Kamenev** voted against the October Revolution.

front: Which country funded Lenin's journey back to Russia?
back: Lenin's journey back to Russia was funded by **Germany**, who believed his presence would force Russia to surrender in the First World War.

front: Which cruiser fired on the Winter Palace during the October Revolution?
back: The cruiser **'Aurora'** fired on the Winter Palace during the October Revolution.

front: After the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks had control of <u>     </u> but not the whole of Russia.
back: After the October Revolution, the Bolsheviks had control of **Petrograd** but not the whole of Russia.

front: In 1928, the Bolsheviks commissioned <u>          </u> to create a film about the October Revolution.
back: In 1928, the Bolsheviks commissioned **Sergei Eisenstein** to create a film about the October Revolution.

front:
**True or False?**

The Bolsheviks faced heavy resistance storming the guarded gates of the Winter Palace.
back:
**False.**

In reality, the gates of the Winter Palace were unguarded and open, and the Bolsheviks faced little resistance.

front:
**True or False?**

Stalin played a major role in the October Revolution.
back:
**False.**

Stalin was a minor member of the Bolshevik Party and played a little role in the October Revolution.

front: Define **Cheka**.
back: The **Cheka** was the secret police force created by Lenin to target 'counter-revolutionary' enemies of the Bolsheviks.

front: Define **Sovnarkom**.
back: The **Sovnarkom** was the Council of People's Commissars, a governing body made up entirely of Bolsheviks and chaired by Lenin.

front: Define **grain requisition**.
back: **Grain requisition** was the seizing of grain from the peasants by Red Army soldiers, used as a terror tactic during the Civil War.

front: Who did Lenin place in total control of the Red Army?
back: Lenin placed **Trotsky** in total control of the Red Army.

front: Who did Trotsky enlist to train the Red Army?
back: Trotsky enlisted **ex-tsarist officers** to train the Red Army, monitored closely by political commissars.

front: Which railway did the Bolsheviks control to move troops across Russia?
back: The Bolsheviks controlled access to the **Trans-Siberian railway**, allowing easy movement of troops and equipment.

front: Why did the White Army's connection to Britain and France harm them?
back: The connection harmed the White Army because **many Russians did not trust Europeans or Western powers**, which Bolshevik propaganda exploited.

front: Which two key industrial centres did the Red Army hold?
back: The Red Army held the key industrial centres of **Moscow and Petrograd**, which they used to gain troops and resources.

front: Trotsky reinstated the <u>        </u> for desertion or disloyalty to the Red Army.
back: Trotsky reinstated the **death penalty** for desertion or disloyalty to the Red Army.

front: Trotsky used the slogan '<u>              </u>' to recruit soldiers to the Red Army.
back: Trotsky used the slogan '**Everything for the Front**' to recruit soldiers to the Red Army.

front:
**True or False?**

The different groups within the White Army shared the same aim.
back:
**False.**

The White Army's groups did not have the same aim, and a hatred of Bolsheviks was not enough to unify them.

front:
**True or False?**

The Allies supported the White Army during the Civil War.
back:
**True.**

The Allies supported the White Army, hoping Russia would form a moderate government that continued the war effort.

front: Define **War Communism**.
back: **War Communism** was the communist approach to the economy introduced by the Bolsheviks in June 1918 during the Civil War, under which the government took control of all areas of production.

front: Define **grain requisitioning**.
back: **Grain requisitioning** was the seizing of peasants' grain under War Communism, which combined with poor weather to cause the **Great Famine** of 1921-1922.

front: Define **tax in kind**.
back: The **tax in kind** was the NEP policy that replaced grain requisitioning, under which peasants gave **50% of their grain to the state** and could sell any surplus.

front: Define **NEPmen**.
back: **NEPmen** were the traders created under the NEP when peasants were allowed to sell their surplus grain on the open market.

front: Which 1921 event forced Lenin to abandon War Communism?
back: The **Kronstadt Uprising** of 1921 forced Lenin to abandon War Communism.

front: Who assembled 20,000 Red Army soldiers to crush the Kronstadt Uprising?
back: **Trotsky** assembled 20,000 Red Army soldiers to crush the Kronstadt Uprising.

front: Under the NEP, which type of industry did the state keep control of?
back: Under the NEP, the state kept control of large-scale **heavy industry**, along with transport and the banking system.

front: By what year had production reached pre-war levels under the NEP?
back: Under the NEP, production reached pre-war levels by **1926**.

front: Grain requisitioning combined with poor weather caused the Great Famine of <u>     </u>.
back: Grain requisitioning combined with poor weather caused the Great Famine of **1921-1922**.

front: In 1921, Lenin signed an <u>        </u> trade agreement, increasing foreign trade.
back: In 1921, Lenin signed an **Anglo-Russian** trade agreement, increasing foreign trade.

front:
**True or False?**

The Kronstadt sailors' mutiny in 1921 was pro-Bolshevik.
back:
**False.**

The 1921 Kronstadt mutiny was anti-Bolshevik; it was the earlier July 1917 mutiny that was pro-Bolshevik.

front:
**True or False?**

Extreme communists in the Bolshevik Party welcomed the NEP.
back:
**False.**

Extreme communists disliked the NEP because NEPmen and kulaks benefited from it.

front: When did Lenin die?
back: Lenin died on **21st January 1924**.

front: Define **Lenin's Testament**.
back: **Lenin's Testament** was the last will Lenin dictated between late 1922 and early 1923, setting out his aims for the Bolshevik Party and criticising leading members including **Stalin** and **Trotsky**.

front: Which party member shot Lenin in 1918?
back: **Fanya Kaplan**, a member of the SRs, shot Lenin twice outside a factory in Moscow.

front: What did Lenin's Testament suggest be done about Stalin?
back: Lenin's Testament suggested that the comrades find a way of **removing Stalin** from his post as General Secretary.

front: In 1921, Stalin became the <u>          </u> of the Bolshevik Party.
back: In 1921, Stalin became the **General Secretary** of the Bolshevik Party.

front: Why did Lenin criticise Trotsky in his Testament?
back: Lenin criticised Trotsky for being **overconfident and arrogant** and for being too focused on the administrative side of work rather than leading the party.

front: Define **permanent revolution**.
back: **Permanent revolution** was the left-wing belief that the USSR needed to **spread communism across the world**, an idea that was unpopular with the party.

front: Define **Socialism in One Country**.
back: **Socialism in One Country** was the right-wing policy of **strengthening communism within the USSR** before pursuing global communism, an idea that was popular with the party.

front: What trick did Stalin play on Trotsky at Lenin's funeral?
back: Stalin **told Trotsky the wrong date** for Lenin's funeral, ensuring Trotsky missed it, while Stalin gave a speech and posed as chief mourner.

front: By <u>     </u> 1929, Stalin was the undisputed leader of the USSR.
back: By **December** 1929, Stalin was the undisputed leader of the USSR.

front:
True or False?

Lenin named Stalin as his successor before he died.
back:
**False.**

Lenin did not name a successor, which led to a power struggle between the left and right wings of the Bolshevik Party.

front: How did Stalin isolate the left wing of the party in 1926?
back: Stalin **allied with Bukharin** to expel Zinoviev and Kamenev, promoting his 'Socialism in One Country' policy.

front: Define **Purges**.
back: The **Purges** were Stalin's campaign of political attacks, arrests and executions used to eliminate perceived enemies and enforce total loyalty across Soviet society.

front: Who was assassinated in 1934, triggering the Great Purge?
back: **Sergei Kirov**, a senior Politburo politician, was assassinated in 1934, which Stalin used to launch the Great Purge.

front: Who assassinated Sergei Kirov?
back: A man named **Leonid Nikolayev** assassinated Kirov in 1934.

front: What political reason did Stalin have for launching the purges?
back: Stalin was **paranoid** that party members with links to Lenin or Trotsky wanted to overthrow him, and he wanted to eliminate all opposition and secure total loyalty.

front: How did the purges help Stalin's economic aims?
back: The purges helped Stalin economically by allowing him to punish those who missed production targets, **forcing people to work harder** and providing **free forced labour** through the GULAG system.

front: Define **saboteurs**.
back: **Saboteurs** were people the state accused of deliberately damaging or obstructing industrial progress, a charge used to justify arrests during the purges.

front: Those arrested were sent to the <u>   </u> system to do forced labour.
back: Those arrested were sent to the **GULAG** system to do forced labour.

front: What happened to the armed forces during the purges?
back: Stalin heavily attacked the armed forces, having **eight senior generals and three out of five marshals shot**, with all three armed forces losing about 50% of their officers.

front: Around <u>  </u> of the Central Committee members in 1934 were arrested and shot.
back: Around **70%** of the Central Committee members in 1934 were arrested and shot.

front: Why did Stalin turn against the NKVD by 1938?
back: Stalin turned against the NKVD because he blamed them for excessive arrests and believed they **knew too much**, executing their head Yagoda and 23,000 officers.

front: How was Trotsky assassinated in 1940?
back: Trotsky was assassinated in Mexico by a Spanish communist named **Ramón Mercader**, who murdered him with an ice pick.

front:
True or False?

The Great Terror is also known as the Yezhovshina.
back:
**True.**

The Great Terror of 1936–1938 is known in Russian as the Yezhovshina.

front: Define **NKVD**.
back: The **NKVD** was the Soviet secret police formed in 1934, tasked with eliminating political enemies and carrying out the Great Purges for Stalin.

front: When was the NKVD formed?
back: The NKVD was formed in **1934**, combining all forms of military and general police into one organisation.

front: From what age could the NKVD prosecute children as adults from 1935?
back: From 1935, the NKVD could prosecute children as young as **12** as adults.

front: Define **GULAG system**.
back: The **GULAG system** was an organisation of forced labour camps, many located in Siberia, used to punish criminals, deter crime and provide the state with free labour.

front: Many of the forced labour camps of the GULAG system were located in <u>    </u>.
back: Many of the forced labour camps of the GULAG system were located in **Siberia**.

front: Why did many prisoners die in the GULAG system?

After the purges, the remaining members of the party and army were loyal to Stalin.

The purges removed potential opponents, leaving the remaining members of the Communist Party and the army loyal to Stalin.

front: Define **Gosplan**.
back: **Gosplan** was the 'State Committee for Planning' that Stalin created to organise the Five-Year Plans, setting targets for each region, factory, manager and worker.

front:

front:
**True or False?**

The targets set by Gosplan were usually realistic and easily achieved.

The targets set by Gosplan were ambitious and usually unachievable.

back: By 1940, women made up **40%** of the workforce.

front: When did the First World War take place?

front: Define **self-determination**.
back: **Self-determination** was Wilson's idea that all national groups should have their own country.

back: The **14 Points** were Woodrow Wilson's plan for a lasting peace, including self-determination, disarmament and a **League of Nations**.

front: Clemenceau wanted the return of the region of <u>         </u> to France.

front: Clemenceau did not believe the treaty restricted Germany's <u>  </u> enough.

The League successfully forced Poland to withdraw its troops from Vilna.

The League punished Italy for invading Corfu but not Greece for invading Bulgaria.

front: Define the **Wall Street Crash**.

front: Define **militarism**.

front: Roughly how many Germans were unemployed during the Depression?

front:
**True or False?**

France was hit less badly by the Depression than other major countries.

France was not hit as badly as other countries, with around 5% unemployment.

front: Define the **Mukden Incident**.

front: What did Japan rename Manchuria after taking control?

front: When did Japan leave the League of Nations?
back: Japan left the League of Nations in **March 1933** after rejecting its decision.

front: Why did Britain and France not want to stand up to Japan?
back: Britain and France did not act because Japan was a **permanent member** that could veto actions, and they had colonies in the Far East that a war would threaten.

front: Where and in which years was the World Disarmament Conference held?
back: The World Disarmament Conference was held in **Geneva, Switzerland, from 1932 to 1934**.

front: When did Hitler take Germany out of the League of Nations?

Hitler and Mussolini now knew that the League would not stop them from achieving their aggressive foreign policy aims.

front: Define the **Stresa Front**.

front: What is Abyssinia known as today?
back: Abyssinia is now known as **Ethiopia**.

front: Where did the border clash that sparked the Abyssinian Crisis take place in 1934?

front: How many soldiers did Italy use to invade Abyssinia in October 1935?

front: Which capital did Italy capture in May 1936?

front: Which alliance did Italy and Germany form in 1936?
back: In 1936, Italy and Germany formed the **Rome-Berlin Axis**.

front:

The League's Health Commission became the World Health Organization within the United Nations.

front: When did the Second World War begin?

front: Why did the USA enter the war in December 1941?

front: Define the **revisionist view** of the war's causes.
back: The **revisionist view** is that Hitler did not want to start a war but was an **opportunist**, and that other world leaders and the Treaty of Versailles were to blame.

front: Which two actions show Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles?
back: Hitler broke the Treaty of Versailles through the **remilitarisation of the Rhineland** and **Anschluss with Austria**.

front: What do revisionist historians believe caused the war?
back: Revisionist historians believe the **Treaty of Versailles caused the war**, as it was harsh enough to make Germans hate it but too weakly enforced.

front: The Holocaust resulted in the murder of <u>    </u> million Jewish people.
back: The Holocaust resulted in the murder of **6** million Jewish people.

front:
**True or False?**

The USA entered the Second World War as soon as it began in 1939.

front: Define **'dolchstoss'**.

front: Define the **'November Criminals'**.
back: The **'November Criminals'** were the politicians who signed the Treaty of Versailles, named after the month the government signed the armistice.

back: By 1923, the British public thought that the treaty was **too harsh on Germany**.

front: Why did Britain want a strong Germany by 1923?
back: Britain wanted a strong Germany to **defend Europe from communism**, as people began to fear the USSR more than Germany.

front: Why did many French citizens dislike the treaty?
back: Many French citizens thought the treaty was **too soft on Germany** and did not feel protected.

front: Define ***Lebensraum***.
back: ***Lebensraum*** meant **'living space'**, the theory that Germany needed more territory in Eastern Europe so its population could grow and communism could be destroyed.

front: Define ***Grossdeutschland***.
back: ***Grossdeutschland*** meant **'Greater Germany'**, the idea that all German speakers should unite under one Reich, including through Anschluss with Austria.

front:

front: When did Germany leave the League of Nations?
