front:
**True or False?**

Unskilled rural workers had plenty of alternative job opportunities when farm prices fell.
back:
**False.**

Unlike unskilled workers in cities, rural workers had few opportunities to find work elsewhere and were often trapped in low-paying jobs.

front: Define **reservations**.
back: **Reservations** were areas of poor-quality land, unsuitable for growing crops, where Indigenous Americans were forced to live in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

front: Define **poverty line**.
back: The **poverty line** is the income level below which a family cannot afford basic needs; in 1929, 60 per cent of American families still lived below it.

front: Which group of Americans benefitted most from the economic boom?
back: Americans who were **male, white and already wealthy** benefitted most from the economic boom.

front: What proportion of American families still lived below the poverty line in 1929?
back: **60 per cent** of American families still lived below the poverty line in 1929.

front: How did the urban middle class benefit from mass production and hire purchase?
back: The urban middle class benefited because **consumer goods became available and affordable**, dramatically improving their standard of living.

front: How were Black Americans treated in the northern job market during the 1920s?
back: Black Americans were often the **last to be hired and first to be fired**, working in the lowest paid sectors.

front: Women continued to be paid <u>  </u> than men for doing exactly the same jobs during the 1920s.
back: Women continued to be paid **less** than men for doing exactly the same jobs during the 1920s.

front: Indigenous Americans had been forced to live on <u>       </u> with poor-quality land.
back: Indigenous Americans had been forced to live on **reservations** with poor-quality land.

front:
**True or False?**

All American women experienced increased wealth and opportunity during the 1920s.
back:
**False.**

Although some wealthy, white, upper-class women benefited, most women did not and continued to be paid less than men.

front:
**True or False?**

Investors who could afford stocks and shares benefitted as the stock market rose throughout the 1920s.
back:
**True.**

The stock market rose throughout the 1920s, so investors benefitted by selling shares for more than they had paid.

front: How were recently arrived immigrants treated in the 1920s job market?
back: Recently arrived immigrants were frequently **discriminated against**, and only the lowest paid jobs were usually available to them.

front: Define the **Roaring Twenties**.
back: The **Roaring Twenties** was a period of rapid cultural, social and economic change in the US during the 1920s.

front: Roughly how many cars were there in the US by 1929?
back: By 1929, there were around **23 million** cars in the US.

front: What made the car industry grow significantly in the 1920s?
back: The car industry grew significantly in the 1920s because of **mass production**.

front: The motor car was invented in the year <u>  </u>.
back: The motor car was invented in the year **1885**.

front: Which entertainment medium became the most popular in the US during the 1920s?
back: During the 1920s, the most popular entertainment medium in the US was the **radio**.

front: Around how many US homes had a radio by 1929?
back: By 1929, around **10 million** homes in the US had a radio.

front:
**True or False?**

Radio was useful because it could reach people who were illiterate.
back:
**True.**

Many people in the US were illiterate in the 1920s, and radio enabled communication to all citizens regardless of whether they could read and write.

front: From which region of the US did jazz music originate?
back: Jazz music originated from the **southern states** of the US.

front: Which internationally famous jazz musician is named in the note?
back: An internationally famous jazz musician of the 1920s was **Louis Armstrong**.

front: A popular new dance developed alongside jazz in the 1920s was the <u>      </u>.
back: A popular new dance developed alongside jazz in the 1920s was the **Charleston**.

front: Define the **Golden Age of Hollywood**.
back: The **Golden Age of Hollywood** is the name given to the 1920s, a decade when cinema flourished before television had been invented.

front: How many cinema visits were Americans making each week by 1929?
back: By 1929, Americans were making **110 million** visits to the cinema every week.

front: Define **WASPs**.
back: **WASPs** were White Anglo-Saxon Protestants, the powerful White Americans descended from North-Western European immigrants who held positions of power in early 20th-century America.

front: Approximately how many people emigrated to the US between 1850 and 1914?
back: Between 1850 and 1914, approximately **40 million** people emigrated to the United States.

front: Which 1924 law reduced the maximum number of immigrants to 154,000 per year?
back: The maximum number of immigrants entering the US each year was reduced to 154,000 by the **Reed–Johnson Act** of 1924.

front: The 1921 <u>         </u> Act limited immigration from the eastern hemisphere.
back: The 1921 **Emergency Quota** Act limited immigration from the eastern hemisphere.

front: Define the **KKK**.
back: The **KKK** (Ku Klux Klan) was a racist organisation formed in the Southern US after the Civil War that believed in white supremacy and attacked, tortured and killed Black Americans.

front: Which 1915 film led to an enormous revival of the KKK?
back: The KKK was revived enormously by the 1915 release of the film **The Birth of a Nation**.

front: Roughly how large was KKK membership by 1925?
back: By 1925, KKK membership had grown to around **5 million** people.

front: In which year was the NAACP founded?
back: The NAACP was founded in **1909**.

front: What was the aim of the NAACP?
back: The NAACP was created to combat **racial injustice on a national scale**.

front: Define **Jim Crow Laws**.
back: **Jim Crow Laws** were laws passed by White politicians in the Southern states that discriminated against Black Americans, forcing them to use separate facilities and preventing many from voting.

front:
**True or False?**

Lynchings of Black Americans in the South were usually investigated and punished by the police.
back:
**False.**

These murders were usually not investigated by the police, and the murderers went unpunished.

front: In 1919, there were <u>  </u> lynchings in the Southern US.
back: In 1919, there were **70** lynchings in the Southern US.

front: Define **Prohibition**.
back: **Prohibition** was a nationwide ban that made the production, selling and distribution of alcohol illegal across the US.

front: Which amendment made the sale of alcohol illegal?
back: The sale of alcohol was made illegal by the **18th Amendment**.

front: The <u>     </u> Act classified alcohol as any drink that had contained more than 0.5% alcohol.
back: The **Volstead** Act classified alcohol as any drink that had contained more than 0.5% alcohol.

front: Between which years did Prohibition last in the US?
back: Prohibition began in 1920 and lasted until **1933**.

front: Which two temperance groups campaigned for Prohibition?
back: The two temperance groups that campaigned for Prohibition were the **Anti-Saloon League and the Women's Christian Temperance Union**.

front: Which industrialist supported Prohibition because he believed alcohol reduced workers' efficiency?
back: The industrialist who supported Prohibition because he believed alcohol reduced efficiency was **Henry Ford**.

front:
**True or False?**

Some religious groups, such as the Methodists and Baptists, supported Prohibition because they believed drinking alcohol was a sin.
back:
**True.**

The Methodists and Baptists did not agree with drinking alcohol and believed that drinking alcohol was a sin.

front: Define **bootlegging**.
back: **Bootlegging** was the illegal activity of people making and selling alcohol secretly during Prohibition.

front: Which gangster became a powerful figure by smuggling and distributing alcohol?
back: The gangster who became a powerful figure by smuggling and distributing alcohol was **Al Capone**.

front: Bootleggers paid police officers <u>    </u> to ignore their illegal activities.
back: Bootleggers paid police officers **bribes** to ignore their illegal activities.

front: Which US President repealed the 18th Amendment in 1933?
back: The 18th Amendment was repealed in 1933 by President **Roosevelt**.

front: How did the Great Depression contribute to the end of Prohibition?
back: The Great Depression led to mass unemployment, and legalising alcohol production would **create more jobs**.

front: Define **flappers**.
back: **Flappers** were young women in 1920s America who rejected traditional expectations by cutting their hair short, wearing short skirts, using bold makeup, smoking and drinking.

front: What jobs did women commonly take when American men left to fight from 1917?
back: When men left to fight from 1917, women took on male-dominated jobs such as working in **munition factories and heavy industry**.

front:
**True or False?**

Before the First World War, most women worked outside the household.
back:
**False.**

Most women did not work outside of the household, and those who did had stereotypical jobs such as being a seamstress or a maid.

front: In which year did American women win the right to vote in general elections?
back: American women won the right to vote in general elections in **1920**.

front: Women won the right to vote through the passing of the <u>  </u> Amendment.
back: Women won the right to vote through the passing of the **19th** Amendment.

front: Define the **Maternity and Infancy Protection Act**.
back: The **Maternity and Infancy Protection Act** (1921) provided federal and state funds to prevent the deaths of mothers and babies during childbirth.

front: By how much did the number of American women with jobs increase between 1920 and 1929?
back: By 1929, **25% more** American women had jobs than in 1920.

front: What happened to the divorce rate during the 1920s?
back: During the 1920s, the divorce rate **doubled**.

front: Roughly how many women worked outside the home in 1929?
back: In 1929, around **10.9 million** women worked in jobs outside of the home.

front: What backgrounds did almost all flappers come from?
back: Flappers were almost all **white, wealthy, upper-class women** from cities in the northern states.

front: Most employed women were in low-skilled jobs and were paid <u>  </u> than men for the same work.
back: Most employed women were in low-skilled jobs and were paid **less** than men for the same work.

front: Why did most women's lives not change much despite the flapper image?
back: Most women continued to have children early and bore nearly all of the burden of **childcare**, while management positions and politics remained closed to them.

front: Define **Speculation**.
back: **Speculation** is when a person buys something in the hope that its value will increase, so they can sell it later at a higher price to make a **profit**.

front: Define **Wall Street**.
back: **Wall Street** is the name given to the **US Stock Exchange**.

front: What did buying shares 'on the margin' mean?
back: Buying shares 'on the margin' meant that investors only paid for about **10 per cent** of the shares and borrowed the money to pay for the rest.

front: Buying shares by paying only around 10 per cent up front and borrowing the rest was called buying 'on the <u>      </u>'.
back: Buying shares by paying only around 10 per cent up front and borrowing the rest was called buying 'on the **margin**'.

front: On what date did the Wall Street Crash begin?
back: The Wall Street Crash began on **24 October 1929**, which became known as 'Black Thursday'.

front: By what name did 24 October 1929 become known?
back: 24 October 1929 became known as **Black Thursday**.

front: How many shares were sold on the New York Stock Exchange on 24 October 1929?
back: On 24 October 1929, **13 million shares** were sold on the New York Stock Exchange.

front: Approximately <u>        </u> shares were sold on 29 October 1929 as prices continued to fall.
back: Approximately **16 million** shares were sold on 29 October 1929 as prices continued to fall.

front: How many American banks went bust in 1929?
back: A total of **659 American banks** went bust in 1929.

front: Which three underlying economic problems caused the US economy to slow in 1929?
back: The US economy slowed in 1929 because of **low exports**, **uneven income distribution** and **overproduction of consumer goods**.

front: What did the Wall Street Crash of 1929 trigger?
back: The Wall Street Crash of 1929 triggered the **Great Depression**.

front:
True or False?

People who bought shares 'on the margin' had paid for the shares in full.
back:
**False.**

They only paid for about 10 per cent of the shares and **borrowed** the money to pay for the rest.

front: Define **Hobos**.
back: **Hobos** were people who travelled from state to state looking for work during the Great Depression.

front: By how much had industrial production fallen by 1932?
back: By 1932, industrial production had fallen by **45%**.

front: By how much had car production fallen by 1932?
back: By 1932, car production had fallen by **80%**.

front: How many businesses went bankrupt between 1929 and 1932?
back: Over **100,000 businesses** went bankrupt between 1929 and 1932.

front: Share prices did not stop falling for <u>      </u> years after the crash.
back: Share prices did not stop falling for **three** years after the crash.

front: Why did many savers rush to withdraw their money after the crash?
back: Many savers rushed to withdraw all their savings **before their bank went bust**, which made the situation for banks even worse.

front: Why did banks struggle in the aftermath of the crash?
back: Banks struggled because too many loans had been given to people to buy shares **'on the margin'** before the crash.

front: How many farmers lost their land during the Great Depression?
back: Around **750,000 farmers** lost their land during the Great Depression.

front: Why did farmers' loan repayments become more expensive after 1929?
back: Farmers' loan repayments became more expensive because **interest rates increased** between 1929 and 1932.

front: By 1933, around one in <u>      </u> US citizens (14 million) were unemployed.
back: By 1933, around one in **four** US citizens (14 million) were unemployed.

front: Why did many coal mines close during the Depression?
back: Many coal mines closed because **demand for coal fell** as fewer factories required power and heating.

front:
True or False?

Unemployed Americans received welfare and unemployment benefits during the Depression.
back:
**False.**

There were **no welfare or unemployment benefits** for those who had lost their jobs, yet rent and mortgages still had to be paid.

front: Define **Hoovervilles**.
back: **Hoovervilles** were settlements of temporary housing built on wasteland out of whatever materials people could find, named as an attack on **President Hoover**.

front: Define **Sharecroppers**.
back: **Sharecroppers** were farmers who had to give part of their crop to a landowner as rent.

front: Define **Dust Bowl**.
back: The **Dust Bowl** was when drought conditions combined with strong winds on the Great Plains in 1930 to blow away the topsoil, decreasing the fertility of millions of acres of farmland.

front: From what percentage to what percentage did unemployment rise between 1929 and 1933?
back: Unemployment rose from **3% in 1929** to **25% in 1933**.

front: Why were the shanty settlements named 'Hoovervilles'?
back: They were named as an attack on **President Hoover** for his government's failure to help people during the Depression.

front: By 1932, over <u>        </u> Americans were unable to repay their mortgages.
back: By 1932, over **250,000** Americans were unable to repay their mortgages.

front: How did employers treat workers who kept their jobs after the crash?
back: Employers **reduced wages** and **increased working hours** for the workers who kept their jobs.

front: Where did many farm workers migrate to in search of jobs?
back: Many farm workers headed to the citrus farms of **California** in search of jobs.

front: What caused the soil erosion in the Midwest?
back: The soil erosion in the Midwest was caused by **overcultivation**.

front: To which northern cities did former sharecroppers move in search of work?
back: Former sharecroppers moved to northern cities such as **Chicago** and **New York** in search of work.

front: In California, some immigrant workers were deported from the US and repatriated to <u>       </u>.
back: In California, some immigrant workers were deported from the US and repatriated to **Mexico**.

front:
True or False?

The US government provided social security to help unemployed workers after the crash.
back:
**False.**

The US had **no social security** in the 1920s, and the Republican government expected unemployed workers to resolve their own problems.

front: Define **Rugged individualism**.
back: **Rugged individualism** was Hoover's belief in self-reliance, the idea that people should solve their own problems and that this would pull America through.

front: Define **Smoot-Hawley tariff**.
back: The **Smoot-Hawley tariff** was a measure introduced by Hoover that increased the price of foreign imports to encourage Americans to buy US goods.

front: What did Hoover declare to the American people in January 1930?
back: In January 1930, Hoover declared that **'we have now passed the worst'**.

front: What was the unintended consequence of the Smoot-Hawley tariff?
back: It caused foreign countries to introduce tariffs on US goods, so **US exports collapsed** and companies went bust.

front: Who were the Bonus Marchers?
back: The Bonus Marchers were a group of **25,000 First World War veterans** who wanted their war pension paid immediately rather than in 1945.

front: The Bonus Marchers set up a Hooverville directly outside the <u>          </u> in March 1932.
back: The Bonus Marchers set up a Hooverville directly outside the **White House** in March 1932.

front: How did the US Army remove the Bonus Marchers?
back: The US Army used **tear gas and tanks** to move the Bonus Marchers, killing two protestors and a baby and injuring more than 1,000 people.

front: Which political party did Franklin D. Roosevelt represent in 1932?
back: Roosevelt was the **Democratic** presidential candidate in 1932.

front: Whom did Roosevelt promise his government would help?
back: Roosevelt promised that his government would help the **'forgotten man'**.

front: What did Roosevelt promise to resolve the Depression?
back: Roosevelt promised a **'New Deal'** to resolve the Depression.

front: In the 1932 election, Roosevelt won the vote in <u>     </u> states, while Hoover won in just six.
back: In the 1932 election, Roosevelt won the vote in **48** states, while Hoover won in just six.

front:
True or False?

Roosevelt won the 1932 election by around 8 million more votes than Hoover.
back:
**True.**

Roosevelt won **8 million more votes** than Hoover in the biggest landslide in US history.

front: Define **New Deal**.
back: The **New Deal** was Franklin D. Roosevelt's radical solution to the problems caused by the Great Depression, which reshaped the relationship between the federal government and the American people.

front: Define **Hundred Days**.
back: The **Hundred Days** refers to the early weeks of Roosevelt's presidency in which he immediately introduced a series of New Deal measures to tackle the Depression.

front: Define **Alphabet Agencies**.
back: The **Alphabet Agencies** were the government bodies created by Roosevelt to tackle specific problems of the Depression, each known by its abbreviation.

front: Define **boondoggles**.
back: **Boondoggles** were the pointless jobs created by the Civil Works Administration, such as hiring 100 people in Washington to scare pigeons away with balloons.

front: What were Roosevelt's three key aims for the New Deal?
back: Roosevelt's three key aims for the New Deal were **relief, recovery and reform**.

front: What did the Emergency Banking Act do to all banks in 1933?
back: The Emergency Banking Act **closed all banks for four days** and ordered their accounts to be inspected.

front: Which symbol could businesses that met NRA promises display on their products?
back: Businesses that met NRA promises could display the **Blue Eagle** on their products.

front: Which agency paid farmers to produce less?
back: The **Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA)** paid farmers to produce less.

front: How were Roosevelt's radio broadcasts to the American people known?
back: Roosevelt's radio broadcasts to the American people were known as his **fireside chats**.

front: The Civilian Conservation Corps provided temporary work to single, unemployed men aged <u>  </u> to 25.
back: The Civilian Conservation Corps provided temporary work to single, unemployed men aged **18** to 25.

front:
**True or False?**

The Tennessee Valley Authority built dams to prevent the Tennessee River from flooding.
back:
**True.**

The TVA built 16 hydroelectric dams by 1944 to prevent flooding and soil erosion, and also provided cheap hydroelectricity.

front:
**True or False?**

The Economy Act increased the wages of all government employees.
back:
**False.**

The Economy Act cut the wages of all government employees by 15%, including Roosevelt's own, which freed up \$1 billion to help the unemployed.

front: Define **Second New Deal**.
back: The **Second New Deal** was the set of reforms introduced by Roosevelt in 1935 that strengthened workers' rights, created a national welfare state and enforced a national minimum wage.

front: In which year did Roosevelt introduce the Second New Deal?
back: Roosevelt introduced the Second New Deal in **1935**.

front: How many Americans were still unemployed in 1935?
back: There were still **11 million** unemployed Americans in 1935.

front: Which body ruled that FDR had overreached his powers as president?
back: The **Supreme Court** ruled that FDR had overreached his powers as president.

front: Which Act of the Second New Deal replaced the NRA?
back: The **National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) of 1935** replaced the NRA.

front: Define **Social Security Act of 1935**.
back: The **Social Security Act of 1935** created a national social welfare system that included old-age pensions, disability payments and unemployment payments.

front: Which Second New Deal body became the US's biggest employer?
back: The **Works Progress Administration (WPA)** became the US's biggest employer.

front: What did the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 enforce?
back: The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 enforced a **minimum wage**, as well as limiting working hours and improving working conditions.

front: The Soil Conservation Act of 1935 replaced the <u>  </u> and helped resolve soil erosion caused by the Dust Bowl.
back: The Soil Conservation Act of 1935 replaced the **AAA** and helped resolve soil erosion caused by the Dust Bowl.

front: The Resettlement Administration of 1935 aimed to move 500,000 families but only resettled about <u>   </u> families.
back: The Resettlement Administration of 1935 aimed to move 500,000 families but only resettled about **5,000** families.

front:
**True or False?**

The Social Security Act's welfare system covered all American workers.
back:
**False.**

The system only covered a third of workers and did not support farmers or workers in private households, with pension payments as low as \$85 a month.

front:
**True or False?**

1936 was a presidential election year, which was one reason the New Deal changed.
back:
**True.**

With the American people set to decide whether to keep or replace FDR in 1936, he wanted to ensure he won the election.

front: Define **small government**.
back: **Small government** is the Republican belief that the government should stay out of people's lives and leave them to succeed or fail on their own.

front: Why did Republicans believe the New Deal was harmful to Americans?
back: Republicans believed the New Deal would make Americans **lazy** and cause them to wait for government handouts.

front: How did Roosevelt help pay for the expensive New Deal?
back: Roosevelt **increased the amount of tax** that wealthy people paid to help pay for the New Deal.

front: Which agency forced business leaders to pay a minimum wage and improve working conditions?
back: The **National Recovery Administration (NRA)** forced business leaders to pay a minimum wage and improve working conditions.

front: Which radical senator argued the New Deal did not go far enough?
back: **Huey Long**, a senator from Louisiana, argued that the New Deal did not go far enough.

front: What did Huey Long want the government to do with wealth over \$5 million?
back: Huey Long argued that every penny a person owned over \$5 million should be **confiscated** by the government and distributed amongst the American people.

front: Define **Supreme Court**.
back: The **Supreme Court** was the body that ruled Roosevelt had broken the rules over how much power a president has by acting through the NRA and AAA.

front: Why did the Supreme Court rule the AAA unconstitutional?
back: The Supreme Court ruled that the AAA had paid farmers to not grow food, which was the **role of the state governments**, not the president.

front: Under Huey Long's plans, the redistributed money would give every family a house, a radio and a <u>  </u>.
back: Under Huey Long's plans, the redistributed money would give every family a house, a radio and a **car**.

front: The Supreme Court ruled that the NRA had tried to set prices and wages that only <u>     </u>, not the president, could do.
back: The Supreme Court ruled that the NRA had tried to set prices and wages that only **Congress**, not the president, could do.

front:
**True or False?**

All opposition to the New Deal argued that it went too far.
back:
**False.**

Some opponents, such as the radical Huey Long, argued that the New Deal did not go far enough in correcting the problems in American society.

front:
**True or False?**

Wealthy people resented their taxes being used to help homeless people.
back:
**True.**

Wealthy people deeply resented their money being used to plant trees or being given to homeless people.

front: How many Americans were unemployed when Roosevelt became president in 1933?
back: There were **12.8 million** unemployed Americans when Roosevelt became president in 1933.

front: How many Americans were unemployed by 1941?
back: By 1941, unemployment had been slashed to **5.6 million** Americans.

front: What level did unemployment never fall below during the 1930s?
back: Unemployment never fell below **10 per cent** during the 1930s.

front: Why did improvements in manufacturing contribute to continued unemployment?
back: Improvements in manufacturing meant that **fewer workers** were needed to produce goods.

front: Define **disposable income**.
back: **Disposable income** is the spare money workers can spend on consumer goods, which many Americans lacked because unemployment was high and wages were low.

front: What happened to sales of consumer goods such as cars and radios?
back: Sales of consumer goods such as cars, radios, vacuum cleaners and refrigerators were **low** because workers lacked disposable income.

front: What event finally dragged America out of the Great Depression?
back: The **outbreak of the Second World War** in 1939, and the US's entry in 1941, finally dragged America out of the Great Depression.

front: What did car factories begin producing during the Second World War?
back: Factories that had been built to make cars were soon making thousands of **planes, tanks and guns**.

front: By 1944, there were just <u>    </u> unemployed Americans.
back: By 1944, there were just **670,000** unemployed Americans.

front: Tariffs on US goods affected <u>    </u>, which was one reason unemployment continued.
back: Tariffs on US goods affected **exports**, which was one reason unemployment continued.

front:
**True or False?**

The Second World War almost eliminated unemployment in the US.
back:
**True.**

The combined effect of booming industry and agriculture and people joining the armed forces almost eliminated unemployment, falling to 670,000 by 1944.

front:
**True or False?**

Low consumer spending had no effect on unemployment.
back:
**False.**

Low sales of consumer goods led to the closure of businesses that made them and contributed to the persistently high unemployment figures.

front: Who was appointed by Roosevelt as the first woman to hold a US cabinet job?
back: **Frances Perkins** was appointed by Roosevelt as Secretary of Labor, the first woman in history to have a cabinet job in the US government.

front: Which agency reduced the number of farmers losing their land and improved profits?
back: The **Agricultural Adjustment Administration (AAA)** reduced the number of farmers losing their land and improved profits.

front: Which party did more Black Americans support after the New Deal?
back: After the New Deal, more Black Americans supported the **Democrats**, having previously supported the Republican Party.

front: How many US citizens remained unemployed by 1939?
back: By 1939, **9.5 million** US citizens remained unemployed.

front: Which type of worker did the New Deal benefit more, skilled or unskilled?
back: The New Deal benefitted **skilled** workers more than unskilled workers.

front: How did the NRA treat women's wages?
back: The NRA purposefully set wages **lower for women** than for men.

front: Define **sharecroppers**.
back: **Sharecroppers** were farmers who, when the AAA encouraged reduced production, were forced to leave farming and head to industrial cities to find work.

front: Why did Roosevelt refuse to pass an anti-lynching bill?
back: Roosevelt refused to pass the anti-lynching bill because he needed the support of **southern Democrats** who supported White supremacy.

front: The Civilian Conservation Corps had <u>      </u> camps for Black workers.
back: The Civilian Conservation Corps had **segregated** camps for Black workers.

front: After 1935, many vulnerable people in society benefitted from the <u>         </u> Act.
back: After 1935, many vulnerable people in society benefitted from the **Social Security** Act.

front:
**True or False?**

The New Deal treated Black and white workers equally under the NRA.
back:
**False.**

The NRA paid Black workers less than white workers, and many Black Americans continued to work in low-paying jobs.

front:
**True or False?**

The Works Progress Administration employed women during the Second New Deal.
back:
**True.**

The WPA employed women, though it mainly gave them unskilled jobs.
